Patient presents with persistent low-grade fever, headache for 3 days. Reports general malaise and occasional chills but no significant weight loss or night sweats. Physical examination reveals a slightly fatigued appearance; vital signs are stable: temperature normal (98°F), blood pressure within the lower range of acceptable limits.

Recent travel history noted to an area with known infectious diseases, patient had close contact while there. No recent changes in medication regimen and allergy profile remains consistent—regular diet maintained without dietary restrictions or supplements added during this period; sleep patterns disrupted due mainly by fatigue but overall adequate rest achieved despite some difficulty falling asleep initially each night.  Neuro examination unremarkable: cranial nerves intact, motor strength normal throughout the extremities with no muscle atrophy. Cardiovascular exam reveals a regular rhythm and rate without murmurs or gallops noted upon auscultation; lungs clear to bronchophony bilaterally in all fields of view on inspection (FOV).  Abdominal examination shows soft abdomen free from guarding pain, rebound tenderness not elicited during palpatory assessment.  Skin evaluation demonstrates dryness with no active rashes observed. No significant lesions detected and none appear tender upon light pressure application; there is an absence noted for any notable enlargement or masses within the regional lymph nodes (LNs).

Patient complains of erythematous rhinorrhea accompanied by nasal discharge, which has been ongoing since yesterday evening following a recent bout with influenza A infection. Nasal mucosa appears swollen and edematious upon inspection; there is evidence suggestive on both sides that turbinate hypertrophy may be present.  A history reveals the use over-the-counter (OTC) decongestant administered twice daily, along side an antihistamine for symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis symptoms. Reports experiencing a productive cough with yellowish sputum consistent throughout this illness; patient also mentions frequent episodes necessitating inhaler usage to manage acute bronchospasm.  Smoking history significant—patient is classified as heavy smoker (1 pack per day) and reports chronic exposure, particularly during nighttime hours when sleeping in an environment containing cigarette smoke. Auscultation of the lungs reveals bilateral rhonchi without evidence for wheezing or stridor; however peripheral crackles noted upon ausculatatory examination.  Patient also presents with visual disturbances including papilledema observed on fundoscopic exam and nystagmus elicited during a head movement test, both suggestive symptoms warranting further investigation.
